terms.gloss: literal, used in its own sense (of a word)
evidence: Quint. 8.3.24: cum sint autem verba propria, ficta, trānslāta
Gell. 9.1.8: ūtī verbō propriē (Lewis & Short s.v. proprius)
terms.comment: A word used in its proper sense is verbum proprium, against trānslātum, figurative. Literally is propriē: magis propriē nihil possum dīcere (Cic. Phil. 2.77, Lewis & Short); Pōniturne «arma» propriē an figūrātē?, is “arma” used literally or figuratively? (Traupman 239).

evidence: Cic. Fin. 1.4: fābellae Latīnae ad verbum dē Graecīs expressae (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Of a translation or a quotation that follows the words exactly; Cicero also says verbum prō verbō reddere (Opt. Gen. 14) and verbum ē verbō for a single word rendered exactly (Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: cum sint autem verba propria, ficta, trānslāta, propriīs dignitātem dat antīquitās
phrases.english: and since words are literal, coined or figurative, age gives dignity to the literal ones
Is “arma” used literally or figuratively? — Figuratively.

sources: Lewis & Short: proprius · Lewis & Short: verbum
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency (printed page numbers): p. 239; p. 247; p. 340.
Quintilian checked against the Perseus Latin texts, and cited by its numbering.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
